after: ## Content area 1: the decline of the Qing and the 1911 Revolution
alt: A vertical timeline colour-coded by type. External pressure: the First Opium War and Treaty of Nanjing (1839-42), the Second Opium War (1856-60), defeat by Japan and the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1894-95), the scramble for concessions (1897-98) and the Boxer Uprising and Protocol (1899-1901). Internal crisis: the Taiping Rebellion (1850-64), which shifted power to provincial leaders.
caption: Foreign defeats and the Taiping Rebellion weakened the dynasty over sixty years.

after: ## Content area 1: the decline of the Qing and the 1911 Revolution
alt: Three reforms with their outcomes. Self-Strengthening (1860s-1890s) borrowed military and industrial methods without political change and was exposed by defeat in 1895. The Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 was reversed by Cixi's coup. The New Policies of 1901-1911 abolished the examinations, built a new army and created provincial assemblies, but raised expectations and strengthened groups that turned against the dynasty.
caption: The last reform was the most real, and the most dangerous to the dynasty.

after: ## Content area 1: the decline of the Qing and the 1911 Revolution
alt: Three effects of the New Policies, the abolition of the examinations in 1905, a New Army with revolutionary officers and provincial assemblies from 1909, lead into a chain: the railway protection movement of 1911 unites provincial elites, the Wuchang mutiny of 10 October 1911 sets off provincial declarations of independence, and Puyi abdicates in February 1912.
caption: The reforms shaped who acted in 1911; the railway dispute and Wuchang set the timing.

alt: A vertical timeline from Hara Takashi's premiership in 1918 and universal male suffrage in 1925, through the London Naval Treaty and Hamaguchi's shooting in 1930, the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931, the end of party cabinets in 1932, leaving the League in 1933, the army rebellion of 1936, war with China from 7 July 1937, the Tripartite Pact of 1940 and the US oil embargo, to Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941.
caption: Party government gave way step by step to army initiative.

alt: A balance scale. The lighter left pan holds the view that militarism was a deliberate plan. The heavier right pan holds the view of a weak constitutional system, in which the army and navy answered to the emperor and could topple cabinets, together with economic crisis and nationalist violence.
caption: The Meiji Constitution's structure, crisis and violence let the military take over.

after: ## Content area 3: China under Deng Xiaoping, 1976-1997
alt: A short chain at the top: Mao dies in September 1976, the Gang of Four are arrested in October, and the Third Plenum of December 1978 confirms reform and opening. Below, two columns: the economy changed through the household responsibility system, Special Economic Zones, township and village enterprises and the Southern Tour of 1992; politics was not liberalized, with the Democracy Wall ended, the Four Cardinal Principles of 1979 and the clearing of Tiananmen Square on 4 June 1989.
caption: Separate economic change from political change under Deng.

alt: An essay plan with a thesis that the New Policies were the most important reason for the fall of the Qing. Four paragraphs follow: the reforms (the named factor), foreign pressure, revolutionaries and the railway trigger of 1911. The conclusion says the reforms were decisive because they shaped who acted in 1911 and why.
caption: Weigh the named factor against three others, with precise dates.
